title: Properties of definite integrals
examples: When can I use the additivity property for integrals?
How do I check if a function is odd or even?
Can I use King's property if the limits are not symmetric around zero?

explain.say: Today we look at properties of definite integrals. These properties help simplify difficult calculations. We will learn three main rules today.
First we have additivity. If we have an integral from a to c, we can split it up. We can add the integrals from a to b and b to c. The sum equals the original integral.

items: Split into: Integral from a to b
And: Integral from b to c

draw.text: Integral Additivity: $\inta^c f(x) dx = \inta^b f(x) dx + \intb^c f(x) dx$

explain.say: For example, we want to find the integral from zero to five. We can split it at three. The integral becomes the sum from zero to three and three to five.

draw.text: Example: $\int0^5 f(x) dx = \int0^3 f(x) dx + \int3^5 f(x) dx$

explain.say: Next we look at even and odd functions. An even function has $f(-x)$ equal to $f(x)$. An odd function has $f(-x)$ equal to minus $f(x)$.
If we integrate an odd function over a symmetric interval like minus a to a, the result is zero. For instance, integrating $x^3$ from minus two to two gives zero.

items: Odd function over [-a, a] is zero

draw.text: Odd function over $[-a, a]$ is zero.

faq.q: What does additivity really mean for integrals?
faq.a: It means you can break a single integral into multiple smaller integrals. You just add the results together to get the original value. You can also write it as $\inta^c f(x) dx = \inta^b f(x) dx + \intb^c f(x) dx$.
asks: Can I split the limits of integration?
How do I use the additivity property?

faq.q: When is an even function useful with integrals?
faq.a: If you integrate an even function over a symmetric interval, you can calculate it as two times the integral from zero to the upper limit. This often simplifies the calculation. For example, $\int{-a}^a f(x) dx = 2 \int0^a f(x) dx$.
asks: What is the rule for even functions?

faq.q: What is King's property, and when do I use it?
faq.a: King's property states that $\inta^b f(x) dx = \inta^b f(a+b-x) dx$. This is useful when the function has symmetry around the midpoint of the limits. For example, $\int0^L f(x) dx = \int0^L f(L-x) dx$.
asks: What is the property $\inta^b f(x) dx = \inta^b f(a+b-x) dx$?

faq.q: Do I have to use these properties every time?
faq.a: No, these are tools to simplify problems. If direct integration is easier, you should use that method. Use these properties when the function or limits suggest a simplification is possible. Always check the function type first.
asks: When is it better not to use these properties?

faq.q: What happens if I use additivity incorrectly?
faq.a: If you incorrectly split the integral, the value you calculate will not match the original integral. Always ensure the function $f(x)$ is defined and continuous across the point where you split the integral. Remember the property is additive.
asks: What is the condition for splitting integrals?
Can I split at a point where the function is undefined?

facts: The additivity property allows splitting an integral at any point $b$ between $a$ and $c$.
If $f(x)$ is an odd function, then $\int{-a}^a f(x) dx = 0$.
For an even function $f(x)$, $\int{-a}^a f(x) dx = 2 \int0^a f(x) dx$.
King's property shows $\inta^b f(x) dx = \inta^b f(a+b-x) dx$ for any function $f$.
These properties are useful for simplifying definite integrals without direct evaluation.

quiz.say: Evaluate $\int{- rac{3}{2}}^{ rac{3}{2}} (x^4 + 2x^2) dx$ using function properties.
quiz.why: Since $x^4 + 2x^2$ is an even function, we use $2 \int0^{3/2} (x^4 + 2x^2) dx$, which correctly yields $189/8$.

wrong.0: This is the result if you mistakenly treated the function as odd.
wrong.1: This error occurs when you forget to multiply the result by two.
wrong.2: This mistake happens if you incorrectly use the upper limit in the final step.

wrong.1: This mistake occurs if you incorrectly apply the additivity property instead of King's property.
